topic: The Knowledge Vault: How MLPs in Transformers Store Facts
target_audience: University students in Computer Science or Data Science with basic linear algebra knowledge

sections.title: The Mystery of Model Memory
sections.content: Introduce the concept that while Attention mechanisms handle relationships between words, the Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) layers act as the 'long-term memory' or 'knowledge store' of the Transformer. Frame the central question: Where does the model keep the fact that 'The capital of France is Paris'?
sections.example: Imagine a librarian (the Transformer) walking through a giant library. The Attention mechanism is the librarian's eyes looking at the current book, but the MLP is the rows of bookshelves containing the actual data.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Residual Stream Conveyor Belt
sections.content: Explain the 'Residual Stream' as a continuous flow of information (a vector) that passes through each layer. The MLP doesn't replace this information; it 'reads' from it and 'writes' updates to it via addition.
sections.example: A conveyor belt carries a white box labeled 'Subject: France'. As it passes the MLP station, a robot arm adds a sticker saying 'Capital: Paris' to the side of the box.

sections.title: The First Layer: Pattern Matching (The Keys)
sections.content: Introduce the first linear transformation (W1). Mathematically, this is a set of 'Key' vectors. When the input vector (the query) aligns with a Key vector through a dot product, it 'activates'. Use a graphical representation of vectors pointing in similar directions to show 'matching'.
sections.example: If the input vector represents 'The capital of...', it triggers a specific neuron in W1 that specifically recognizes 'Geopolitical Capitals'.

sections.title: The Activation Gate: Filtering Knowledge
sections.content: Discuss the non-linear activation function (like GELU or ReLU). Explain that this acts as a threshold: if the 'Key' matches well enough, the gate opens; if not, the information is suppressed. This prevents irrelevant 'facts' from being added to the stream.
sections.example: Think of a security guard who only allows people with a 'Paris-shaped' key to pass through the gate to the next room.

sections.title: The Second Layer: Retrieving the Fact (The Values)
sections.content: Introduce the second linear transformation (W2). Each neuron in the first layer is associated with a 'Value' vector in the second layer. If a Key is activated, its corresponding Value (the actual factual data) is projected back into the residual stream.
sections.example: Once the 'Capital Pattern' key is matched, the model pulls the specific 'Paris' vector out of its 'Value' drawer and adds it to the information package on the conveyor belt.

sections.title: Summary: The Key-Value Memory Store
sections.content: Synthesize the process: Input -> Match Key (W1) -> Gate (Activation) -> Retrieve Value (W2). Explain that a Transformer has millions of these tiny 'Key-Value' pairs distributed across layers, forming a massive, programmable associative memory.
sections.example: A visual flow-chart: 'Input: Eiffel Tower' -> 'W1: Recognizes Landmark' -> 'GELU: High Confidence' -> 'W2: Adds [Location: Paris]' -> 'Output: Paris'.
